subject: Comparison of brain circuitry differences between patients with schizophrenia and healthy volunteers

messages.author: 341afaf0beb2dca4
messages.subject: Comparison of brain circuitry differences between patients with schizophrenia and healthy volunteers
parts:
I successfully installed Lavaan and ran the analysis on the supplied data. I consulted the group comparison overview in the author's tutorial but was unsure how to relate my neuroanatomic view of group differences to the statistical terms: I expect healthy to have a different set of brain regions correlated with prefrontal cortex than patients. . The Lavaan example has two schools (analogous to healthy and schizophrenic) and three factors, visual textual speed,each with three measures (analogous to prefrontal, cingulate and striatal each with three regions). 

I want to test if patients and healthy subjects have significantly  different latent variables. Using the school example, I might hypothesize that the x2 visual measure in normals was found under the speed group of latent variables in patients.
How can I test this and how can I get a p value to show that the latent variable structure is different in the two groups? Or in neuroanatomic terms, in schizophrenia, Brodmann area 10 in the prefrontal group is found related to the anterior cingulate, but not in the healthy group?

A second class of hypotheses to be tested is that (for example with the school data)  x2 is part of the visual factor in normals but missing or of much lower association in the patient group. How can I get a p value to test this?

Using package  fa, I got a different factor structure in the two groups, but was uncertain how to test whether the factor structures were significantly different or how to test whether one of the three factors was the one that was different.
I removed the mean value for each brain region of interest from the healthy and from the patients, to remove level differences. But then the factor scores in comparing the two groups had a mean of zero in each group and t.test comparison of factor scores did not seem possible. 

My brain imaging data appears  like the HolzingerSwineford1939 data set. I have two patient groups, healthy and patients (analogous to two schools) and three groups of brain regions (prefrontal, cingulate and striatal each with three representative regions ( analogous to visual, textual, speed, each with three measures x1 x2 x3).  . But school is not in anova example under multiple groups. How can I answer the question of how the groups differ?
Do the schools differ in how the multiple tests are associated with one another? Suppose I find that visual is related to x4 in addition to x1, x2, and x3 in Pasteur but not Grant-White? How can I test the significance of this?
Can I test if the textual to speed arrow is weaker in Grant-White than Pasteur?


I hope that this is clear enough for someone to answer. I would be glad to recruit a collaborator.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Comparison of brain circuitry differences between patients with schizophrenia and healthy volunteers
parts:
If you have specific models in mind that you want to fit to each group, you can fit them as a multiple-group model.  The two groups can have different factor structures by imposing the appropriate constraints.  For example, if you think x4 measures visual in the first group but not the second, you just fix the second group's loading to zero, while estimating it in the first group:

visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + c(NA, 0)*x4

When you fit the two hypothesized models simultaneously as a multiple-group model, the chi-squared fit statistic will tell you whether the model-implied covariance matrices differ statistically from the observed covariance matrices.  If so, you could consult the modification indices in conjunction with standardized expected parameter changes (EPCs) to see which constrained parameters the data don't seem to corroborate.  



If you want to compare models (e.g., a model with equal factor structure across groups, and a model with different factor structure across groups), then you have 2 possibilities: (a) If they are nested models, then a chi-squared difference test could tell you whether the simpler model fits significantly better than the model with more parameters.  (b)  If the models are not nested, you can compare them using AIC (or BIC).  See the semTools function "net()" for a test of whether models are nested/equivalent.



If you want to test whether specific parameters are higher/lower in one group than the other, then you can also use the chi-squared difference test.  Fit a model where the same factor loading is freely estimated in both groups, then fit another model where you constrain that parameter to equality across groups (by giving it the same label): 
  • Model 1: visual =~ x1 + c(a, b)*x2 + x3
  • Model 2: visual =~ x1 + c(a, a)*x2 + x3
If the change in chi-squared indicates significantly better fit for Model 1, then you can conclude that the parameters differ across groups (so one is higher than the other, for reasons other than sampling fluctuation).



Bear in mind that SEM requires large sample sizes (e.g., minimum 100 per group for a model this size, but probably twice that for parameter estimates with any decent precision -- check your SEs to judge the quality of the estimates).  So if you have adequate Ns, you might have enough power to detect trivial differences, so you could also refer to the approximate fit using CFI, RMSEA, etc.

There is a lot of literature available about SEM model fit -- try searching issues of the SEM journal and the archives of the SEMNET list-serv.  Since your questions are as much about SEM in general as about specific software issues, you could probably find help from a wider and more diverse audience of researchers by posting your problem there.

Terry
